title: Rota's basis conjecture for matroids
formal: For every integer \(n\ge1\), every finite matroid of rank n, and every n bases \(B_1,\ldots,B_n\), can the elements in each B_i be ordered as \(b_{i,1},\ldots,b_{i,n}\) so that, for every j, the set \(\{b_{1,j},\ldots,b_{n,j}\}\) is also a basis?
definitions: A matroid consists of a finite set E and a collection I of independent subsets. The empty set belongs to I; subsets of independent sets are independent; and if A,B are independent with |A|<|B|, some element of B outside A can be added to A while retaining independence. A basis is a maximal independent subset, and the rank is its size, the same for all bases. Input bases may overlap: occurrences in different rows are separately positioned, but a column must contain n distinct independent elements of E. The target concerns arbitrary finite matroids, not only independence of vectors over a field.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the stated proposition, with all its quantifiers and hypotheses. Verification of finitely many parameter values does not establish the universal assertion.
why: A universal exchange principle for independence systems underlying greedy algorithms and matroid optimization.

context_blocks.text: The conjecture asks for a square array whose rows and columns are all bases. It requires an exact decomposition.
Montgomery and Sauermann prove asymptotically optimal packing and covering results in 2025. These allow a vanishing relative error and leave the exact n-column assertion open.
